transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The U.S. Supreme Court has for now revived a federal data system the Trump administration
revamped into a tool to check the citizenship of millions of registered voters.
As NPR's Jude Joffe Block reports, the tool had been used by some states before it was
blocked by a federal judge for violating privacy protections.
The federal tool is called SAVE, and the Trump administration made major changes to it last
year, including linking it to social security data for the first time.
But the tool has mistakenly flagged some U.S. citizens as potential non-citizens, leading
them to be taken off state voter rolls as a result.
A federal judge in June said the modified version of SAVE trampled on the privacy rights
of Americans and threatened the right to vote.
But the Supreme Court lifted that block and opened the door for the new SAVE tool to be
used in the lead-up to the election for individualized determinations of citizenship.
Federal law bars systematic purges of voter rolls this close to an election.
Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
Presidents Trump and Xi Jinping are not saying much publicly.
They discussed U.S.-China tensions over trade, Taiwan, and artificial intelligence during
business hours.
But in public, the leaders of the world's two biggest economies have been light on details,
other than Xi's announcement of more meetings to come.
And Paris Rob Schmitz has been covering Xi's first state visit to the U.S. in more than
a decade.
President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan for tea
at the White House.
Xi framed the meetings as productive and substantive, while President Trump said the discussions
would bring "great things" for both countries and that "farmers will be happy," but neither
leader elaborated on the details of what was actually discussed during roughly three hours
of meetings on Thursday.
Xi Jinping said he looked forward to meeting President Trump two more times this year,
first at the APEC meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in November and again at the G20
meeting in Miami in December.
Rob Schmitz, NPR News, Washington.
People on the big island of Hawaii are under a hurricane watch.
Hurricane Nolop is expected to bring rain that can be measured not just in inches but
in feet.
Here's NPR's Bill Chappell.
Hurricane Nolop is not expected to make landfall on Hawaii's big island, but it's coming
close enough to drop up to nearly three feet of rain in some areas over the weekend, according
to the National Hurricane Center.
That can cause dangerous flooding and mudslides.
As of Friday morning, Nolop's maximum winds were around 85 mph, but it's expected to strengthen
into a major storm.
Forecasters say it will also move very slowly, increasing the risk of floods from sustained
heavy rain.
Those are closed on Maui and the big island, some are being used as shelters for people
seeking safety.
Bill Chappell, NPR News.
It's NPR.
Legislation to modernize regulations on mental health guidance for commercial airline pilots
and air traffic controllers has passed the U.S. Senate with bipartisan support.
Many people are still worried that disclosing mental health challenges could lead to professional
setbacks or even costs in their jobs.
The latest bill, passed unanimously yesterday, encourages early disclosure and treatment
while reducing stigma.
The parent company of Florida's Brightline Railroad has filed for bankruptcy protection.
NPR's Joel Rose reports its passenger trains will continue operating during the restructuring.
Brightline has announced a plan to restructure its $5.5 billion debt load in Chapter 11 bankruptcy
proceedings.
The privately owned railroad opened with much fanfare in South Florida eight years ago and
began running its neon yellow trains between Miami and Orlando in 2023.
Ridership has been growing, but not fast enough to make the numbers work.
Brightline says its operating company is not part of the bankruptcy filing and that Florida
trains will continue running.
Still, the filing casts doubt on the future of privately owned passenger rail in the U.S.,
including Brightline West, which aims to connect Las Vegas and Southern California.
Joel Rose, NPR News.
Weekly unemployment claims in the U.S., a proxy for layoffs in the country, have fallen
to their lowest levels since mid-July.
The Labor Department's recorded 197,000 applications for jobless insurance.
The four-week average has also declined.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.
This message comes from Angie.

Don't do that.
Just trust them to get the job done.
